title: The Geography of Polycrisis Resilience
subtitle: Spatial Inequality, Regional Vulnerability and the Geography of Global Resilience
description: A foundational monograph establishing that Polycrisis Resilience must be developed geographically—mapping the spatial distribution of exposure, development…
contribution: Establishes the geographical framework of Polycrisis Resilience—originated by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics—connecting Geographic Exposure, Regional Vulnerability, Resilience Capacity, and Resilience Development across six Global South regions and demographic shifts through 2100.
abstract:
The Geography of Polycrisis Resilience is a foundational publication within the H Heuristics Polycrisis Resilience Series, based on the concept developed by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics (https://polycrisisresilience.hheuristics.com/).
It introduces a four-variable geographical analytical framework—Geographic Exposure, Regional Vulnerability, Resilience Capacity, and Resilience Development—and examines spatial inequality, demographic shifts (2025–2100), and targeted regional development across the Global South.

keyFindings.title: Polycrisis resilience is fundamentally geographical: the capacity of populations, economies, and institutions to withstand interconnected risks is unevenly distributed across environmental conditions, economic development, infrastructure, technology access, and institutional capacity.

Reducing humanity's vulnerability requires directing technological, economic, environmental, and institutional improvements toward the regions where they produce the greatest vulnerability reductions—delivering 8.1x–11.8x social BCRs versus 2.4x for untargeted uniform allocation.

Under UN World Population Prospects 2024, Sub-Saharan Africa's population is projected to grow from ~1.2 billion in 2024 to 2.2 billion by 2054 and 3.3 billion by 2100, making infrastructure and development acceleration faster than demographic growth the central analytical imperative.

The Global South is not homogeneous: Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, MENA, Latin America, and Small Island Developing States face distinct binding geographical constraints requiring tailored resilience development pathways.
